## Supplementary: Mechanism Check {#sec-mechanism}

The action-distribution data confirm that the model's internal mechanics are behaving as expected. Across all steps pooled within each scenario, exploit steps constitute 12.5% of activity for peaked-profile researchers, 47.5% for broad-profile researchers, and 92.4% for flat-profile researchers; training steps constitute 61.0%, 33.9%, and 1.8% respectively; explore steps 26.4%, 18.6%, and 5.8%. The pattern is interpretable. Peaked researchers carry a high training burden (61%) because their nine weak domains (skill ≈ 0.28) fall below the training threshold for most models, triggering sustained training before any exploit can be attempted; they exploit relatively rarely (12.5%) but, when they do, succeed at high niche proficiency. Flat researchers, with a uniform skill of 0.32 sitting just above the training threshold (0.30) for most models, can attempt almost any model directly without training (92.4% exploit) — which produces the high-attempt, mediocre-success dynamic that gives them the highest failure rate. Broad researchers sit between the two. This action-mix gradient — training-heavy for Peaked, exploit-heavy for Flat — is the proximal mechanism behind the monotonic H1 ordering.

Mean actual truthfulness converged to near-identical values across scenarios (.842 / .842 / .839 for Peaked / Broad / Flat), as did the bias gap (.108 / .109 / .111). All three scenarios drive the literature toward a similar aggregate knowledge state; the community structure affects *who fails* along the way, not *where the domain ends up*.

**Skill-frontier dynamics.** The (mean-skill, gap) parameterisation equates per-researcher mean skill *at initialisation*. A separate 30-seed measurement tracked how mean skill evolves over the run. All three scenarios start at a common 0.32, but they diverge:

| Scenario | step 0 | step 100 | step 200 | step 300 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Peaked | 0.319 | 0.354 | 0.385 | **0.409** |
| Broad | 0.319 | 0.333 | 0.346 | **0.353** |
| Flat | 0.320 | 0.322 | 0.327 | **0.331** |

By step 300, Peaked communities have climbed to a mean skill of 0.41, Broad to 0.35, and Flat has barely moved (0.33). The mechanism is the assimilation rule (Equation 7): skill grows by assimilating toward the complexity of existing models, and model complexity is drawn from the publishing researcher's own skill. A Peaked community contains high-skill "summits" — researchers with peak skill ≈ 0.68 — whose published work carries high complexity; everyone else assimilates toward that high-complexity work and the community's skill frontier rises. A Flat community has no summit: every researcher sits at ≈ 0.32, every model carries complexity ≈ 0.32, and there is little above the population to climb toward, so mean skill stagnates.

This divergence is an emergent *consequence* of the distribution shape — a mediator of the effect, not a confound. The reparameterisation removed the *static* mean-skill asymmetry that the earlier design carried at initialisation; the divergence reported here is something the shape manipulation *causes* through the model's dynamics, and it is reported as a substantive finding rather than controlled away. It also means the H1 result has two components, taken up in the Discussion: an *immediate* component (Peaked researchers work at higher niche proficiency from the first step) and a *cumulative* component (Peaked communities raise their whole skill frontier over the run, because concentrated competence produces advanced work that the community learns from).

## Control Check: Flat Skill Distribution {#sec-control}

<!-- VOICE OWNERSHIP: AI-drafted in tier 2.2 (commit e719e33). The four-findings structure ("two sharpen, two complicate") is AI framing — recast in your own structure if it doesn't read like you. -->


The Flat scenario — gap = 0, all researchers uniform at skill 0.32 — is a no-heterogeneity control at the same per-researcher mean as Peaked and Broad. It tests whether the H1 and H2 effects require skill *heterogeneity* (the structural feature the gap manipulates) or merely reflect any non-trivial population dynamic. The control was run under 30 independent seeds matching the main experiment.

**H2: domain concentration requires skill heterogeneity.** The Gini coefficient under Flat profiles was .082 (95% CI [.070, .094]), below both Peaked (.141) and Broad (.099). The full ordering is **Peaked > Broad > Flat**, monotonic in dispersion, with both scenario-vs-Flat contrasts significant (Peaked vs Flat: *d* = 1.88, *p* < .0001; Broad vs Flat: *d* = 0.53, *p* = .005). With uniform profiles, no domain attracts a preferential pull, and the Gini falls to a near-baseline level driven only by stochastic variation. Domain concentration therefore emerges specifically because skill heterogeneity is present, and its magnitude scales with the degree of dispersion.

**H1: the failure-rate ordering is monotonic in skill concentration.** The Flat failure rate was .714 (95% CI [.709, .718]) — the *highest* of the three scenarios. The full ordering is **Peaked (.561) < Broad (.652) < Flat (.714)**, monotonic, with both contrasts very large (Peaked vs Flat: *d* = −5.04, *p* < .0001; Broad vs Flat: *d* = −2.96, *p* < .0001). Replication failure decreases cleanly as competence is concentrated. The action-fraction data explain why: Flat-profile researchers spent 92% of steps in exploitation because a uniform skill of 0.32 sits just above the training threshold (0.30) for most models, allowing direct attempts without training — the combined effect of a high attempt rate and uniformly mediocre proficiency producing the most failed replications. Peaked researchers, by contrast, train heavily before attempting and then exploit at high niche proficiency. The relationship between skill concentration and replication failure is monotonic, not U-shaped: both the dispersed-but-mediocre (Flat) and the moderately-dispersed (Broad) communities fail more than the concentrated (Peaked) one.

**H3: reputation is paced by peak skill.** Flat-profile researchers earned far less reputation (4.35) than either Peaked (11.61) or Broad (9.00); the ordering Peaked > Broad > Flat is again monotonic (Peaked vs Flat *d* = 10.59; Broad vs Flat *d* = 4.83). This confirms the reading in @sec-confirmatory: reputation is bounded by the highest-quality work a researcher can produce, which is set by peak skill. The Flat scenario, with the lowest peak skill (0.32), accumulates the least reputation.

**H4: debunk impact is small and undifferentiated.** Debunk impact rates were ≈.0002 in all three scenarios, with no significant pairwise contrast (all *p* > .4). Under the gradient-aware threshold and quadratic instability boost, debunking is rare and low-impact regardless of skill distribution; the scenarios do not separate on this metric.

Together, the Flat control confirms that the headline findings are properties of skill-distribution *shape*: H1 and H2 both order monotonically across the full dispersion range Peaked → Broad → Flat, and both vanish toward baseline in the no-heterogeneity Flat condition for H2, or reach their worst value there for H1.

## Validation: Parameter Recovery and Empirical Comparison {#sec-validation}

<!-- VOICE OWNERSHIP: AI-drafted in tier 3.1+3.2 (commit 063fdeb). Heavy academic hedging ("interpretable rather than disqualifying", "qualitatively similar ... but at a magnitude below"). Rewrite hedges in your idiom. -->


Two further analyses test the model's methodological standing beyond the sensitivity check below. The first is internal: does the simulation output carry information about its own input parameter? The second is external: does the model produce inequality patterns at the same magnitude as documented in real academic publication distributions? Figure \ref{fig:validation} reports both.

**Parameter recovery.** A grid of six values of the manipulated parameter `gap` (0.00, 0.10, 0.18, 0.28, 0.40, 0.50 — spanning the Flat, Broad, and Peaked conditions and extrapolating beyond) was crossed with 15 random seeds, yielding 90 simulations. From eight outcome metrics per run (replication failure rate, per-domain Gini, per-researcher Gini, mean publications, mean reputation, and the three action fractions), a leave-one-out cross-validated linear regression was fit to predict the underlying gap. Recovery was strong: $R^2 = 0.89$, RMSE = 0.057, Pearson $r = 0.94$ ($p < .0001$). The simulation outputs therefore carry substantial information about the manipulated input parameter — a partial-identifiability check that does not establish full identifiability of the model's many other parameters but does demonstrate that the headline manipulation is recoverable from the observable outputs alone. This is a baseline methodological standard rather than a strong claim, but it rules out the possibility that the H1 and H2 results are an artefact of seed variation rather than being driven by the manipulation.

**Empirical comparison: per-researcher publication inequality.** Across all 90 runs, the Gini coefficient of per-researcher publication counts at simulation end was tightly distributed around $M = 0.39$ (SD = 0.03). The empirical literature on academic productivity reports Gini coefficients of approximately 0.5 to 0.7 for publication counts across active researchers [@Allison1974; @Nielsen2021], with @Nielsen2021 estimating annual citation Gini at 0.65–0.70 in modern data. The model therefore produces qualitatively similar inequality (substantial Gini > 0, with publishing concentrated in a minority of researchers) but at a magnitude below the empirical band. None of the 90 runs fell within [0.50, 0.70].

The undershoot is interpretable rather than disqualifying. Three structural features of the model bound how much inequality it can generate. First, the cull-and-mutate selection rule replaces the bottom 25% of researchers every 40 steps, removing the long left tail of zero-publication careers that contributes substantially to real-world Gini. Second, the simulation runs for 300 steps; real publication-Gini estimates aggregate over multi-decade career horizons during which cumulative-advantage dynamics have far longer to operate. Third, the model lacks the heavy-tailed mechanisms (extreme breakthrough cascades, persistent reputation accumulation without decay, network-driven citation amplification) that produce the most unequal publication distributions empirically. The model therefore produces *cumulative-advantage-flavored* inequality in a *bounded* form, and its 0.39 Gini reflects the shape of the dynamics that are present (skill-bias, salience, reputation) without the tail-driving mechanisms that are absent. A model that exactly reproduced 0.65 would be evidence of fitting; a model that reproduces qualitative inequality at a lower magnitude with an interpretable boundary is evidence of partial empirical correspondence with known limits.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{meta/img/validation_figure.pdf}
\captionsetup{labelformat=apa, labelsep=newline, justification=raggedright}
\caption{\textit{Methodological validation. Panel A: parameter recovery — predicted vs.\ true skill-distribution \texttt{gap} via leave-one-out cross-validated linear regression on outcome metrics ($R^2 = 0.89$, $r = 0.94$, $n = 90$). Panel B: per-researcher publication-Gini distribution across the same 90 runs, with empirical reference band [0.50, 0.70] from Allison \& Stewart (1974) and Nielsen \& Andersen (2021) overlaid in green. Simulated mean = 0.39; the model produces qualitatively similar inequality at a magnitude bounded by structural features of the simulation (cull-and-mutate selection, 300-step horizon, absence of heavy-tailed amplification mechanisms).}}
\label{fig:validation}
\end{figure}
```

Together these analyses sharpen the thesis's methodological standing: the manipulation is recoverable from outcomes (so the H1/H2 results reflect the manipulation, not seed noise), and the model's empirical correspondence is partial and quantitatively bounded rather than implicitly assumed. The Gini undershoot is itself an interpretable claim about which empirical features the present model architecture can and cannot reproduce.

## Layer-Decomposition Ablation {#sec-ablation}

<!-- VOICE OWNERSHIP: AI-drafted in tier 4 (commit 103291b). LONGEST AI-heavy section. Watch for: "honest reading", "structural component", "doing real work here", "interaction effect", repeated bolded sub-claim headers. Rewrite each bolded sub-section in your own voice. -->


A central concern with computational models of this kind is that headline findings can be implicit consequences of architectural choices made when the model was constructed, rather than substantive properties of the system being modelled. To address this concern directly, three nested model layers were run under both the Peaked and Broad scenarios with 15 seeds per cell, yielding 90 additional simulations.

- **L1 — Base dynamics only.** All v1 mechanics on (selection, learning, salience decay, fingerprint drift, breakthrough), but the v2 realism extensions (career stages, social learning, Matthew effect, competitive-pressure bias, misconduct) and the v3 epistemic landscape are disabled.
- **L2 — + Realism.** L1 plus all v2 realism extensions; the landscape remains disabled.
- **L3 — Full v3.** L2 plus the epistemic landscape and its five downstream effects.

Each layer was used to compute the Peaked vs Broad effect size for the two confirmatory metrics. The results reframe what each result is doing in the model.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{meta/img/ablation_figure.pdf}
\captionsetup{labelformat=apa, labelsep=newline, justification=raggedright}
\caption{\textit{Layer-decomposition ablation: Peaked vs Broad means and effect sizes for H1 and H2 across three nested model layers.}
Bars show mean values (95\% CI as error bars) across 15 seeds per cell; Cohen's $d$ and Mann-Whitney significance (\textit{n.s.}, \textit{*}, \textit{**}, \textit{***}) are annotated above each pair.
Panel A: H1 (replication failure rate). Panel B: H2 (per-domain publication Gini).
Both the reversed H1 effect and the H2 effect are present at the base layer and hold at every layer; realism and the landscape modulate the magnitude but do not create the effects.}
\label{fig:ablation}
\end{figure}
```

**The reversed H1 is present at the base architecture.** At Layer 1 — the success-probability rule plus all base dynamics, with no realism extensions and no landscape — the Peaked vs Broad failure-rate gap is already large and in the reversed direction (Peaked .572 < Broad .646; *d* = −2.65). Adding realism (Layer 2) leaves it essentially unchanged (*d* = −3.22); adding the landscape (Layer 3) slightly attenuates it (*d* = −2.03). This is a different ablation profile from the earlier, confounded parameterisation, in which H1 was absent at L1 and emerged only with realism. Under the mean-constant reparameterisation, the reversed H1 is a direct, base-architecture consequence of Equation 1: when total competence is held constant, peaked-profile researchers work at higher niche proficiency and the success-probability rule rewards that proficiency from the first layer onward. This is not the problematic kind of tautology — the effect is transparent (it follows visibly from Equation 1, not from a hidden assumption) and it survives the removal of the skill-bias action-selection rule entirely (Type B, @sec-type-b-results, *d* = −1.68). It is the model's success rule responding correctly to the manipulated variable.

**The H2 effect is large at every layer.** At Layer 1 the Peaked vs Broad difference in per-domain Gini is already substantial (*d* = 1.69). Adding realism leaves it essentially unchanged (Layer 2: *d* = 1.72); adding the landscape slightly attenuates it (Layer 3: *d* = 1.58). H2 is therefore stable across the layer decomposition — the concentration effect is a property of how skill heterogeneity interacts with action selection, present from the base architecture and neither created nor destroyed by the realism or landscape layers. The Type B comparison (@sec-type-b-results) decomposes it further into an architectural and a feedback-emergent component.

**The landscape is not a meta-driver of the headline findings.** A reasonable concern about the model is that the epistemic landscape, with its five downstream effects, might be silently inflating the Peaked/Broad contrasts. The ablation tests this directly: removing the landscape (Layer 2) does not eliminate H1 or H2, and adding it (Layer 3) slightly *attenuates* both rather than amplifying them. The landscape's contribution is to add spatial structure that makes the model's intermediate dynamics interpretable (Figure \ref{fig:landscape}), not to drive the headline findings.

The ablation's methodological implication is that the two confirmatory results are robust to the layer composition. Both the reversed H1 and the H2 concentration effect are present at the base architecture, hold across all three nested layers, and (as the next section shows) survive the replacement of the action-selection rule. They are not artefacts of any single realism extension.

## Type A vs. Type B Architectures: How Much of the Result is Built In? {#sec-type-b-results}

The layer-decomposition ablation (@sec-ablation) addressed one architectural concern by showing that H1 is not produced by Equation 1's profile-mismatch penalty alone. A second, sharper concern remains: the action-selection rule itself (Equation 6, the skill-bias term) directly weights selection toward the researcher's higher-skill domains, which is the mechanism most plausibly responsible for the H2 concentration finding. To test this, both confirmatory metrics were re-evaluated under the Type B architecture defined in @sec-architecture, in which Equation 6 is replaced with a softmax over per-agent Rescorla–Wagner-learned domain utility (Equations 8 and 9). All three scenarios were run with 30 seeds under each mode, yielding 180 simulations of 300 steps. The Rescorla–Wagner parameters were fixed at $\alpha = 0.10$ and $\beta = 3.0$; their robustness is examined in @sec-sensitivity.

**H2 effect drops by roughly a third but does not vanish.** Under Type A, the Peaked vs Broad difference in per-domain Gini is $d = 1.41$ ($p < .0001$; Peaked $= .141$, Broad $= .099$). Under Type B, the same contrast falls to $d = 0.90$ ($p = .001$; Peaked $= .069$, Broad $= .058$). Roughly a third of the H2 effect ($1.41 - 0.90 = 0.51$) depends on the explicit skill-bias rule in Equation 6; when that rule is removed and replaced by softmax-over-learned-utility, the directional result remains, significant, with a magnitude comparable to a large effect. The reading of H2 is therefore that it is *partially architectural* — a $d \approx 0.5$ share reflects the skill-bias action-selection rule's preference for the researcher's peak domain — and *substantially feedback-emergent* — the residual $d \approx 0.9$ under Type B reflects that peaked-profile agents accumulate higher learned utility for their peak domain through the success → reward → utility loop, and the softmax then concentrates publications there. The feedback-emergent component is the larger of the two: concentration is not merely an artefact of the skill-bias rule.

**The reversed H1 effect holds in both modes.** Under Type A, the Peaked vs Broad failure-rate gap is $d = -2.65$ ($p < .0001$; Peaked $= .561$, Broad $= .652$). Under Type B, the gap remains large and in the same reversed direction, $d = -1.68$ ($p < .0001$; Peaked $= .612$, Broad $= .662$). The reversed H1 is therefore robust to the architectural change: removing the skill-bias rule and replacing it with softmax-over-learned-utility does not eliminate or reverse it. This is expected — the H1 reversal traces to Equation 1 (peak proficiency raising niche success probability), which is untouched by the Type A/B switch.

**Within-scenario A-vs-B contrasts.** Type B raises the Peaked failure rate relative to Type A (Peaked: $d = -1.35$, $p < .0001$) and leaves Broad and Flat roughly unchanged (Broad: $d = -0.38$, n.s.; Flat: $d = 0.07$, n.s.); it lowers per-domain Gini concentration in every scenario (Peaked: $d = 3.22$; Broad: $d = 1.79$; Flat: $d = 1.22$; all $p < .0001$). The pattern is interpretable: under Type B, peaked-profile agents must *learn* their peak domain's value through trial-and-reward rather than being directed there by the skill-bias rule, so they spend longer attempting work before their utility vector concentrates — raising their failure rate and lowering their publication concentration relative to Type A.

**Interpretation.** Equation 6 contributes roughly $d \approx 0.5$ to the headline H2 effect of $d \approx 1.4$; the feedback loop contributes the larger remaining $d \approx 0.9$. The reversed H1 is robust to the architectural change (preserved at $d = -1.68$ to $-2.65$ across both modes), consistent with the ablation reading that it is a direct, transparent consequence of the success-probability rule rather than of any action-selection mechanism. The substantive interpretation of these decomposed numbers is taken up in the Discussion.

## Sensitivity Analysis {#sec-sensitivity}

To evaluate the robustness of the confirmatory findings, a one-at-a-time (OAT) sensitivity analysis was conducted. OAT sweeps systematically underestimate parameter importance in nonlinear systems because they do not capture interactions between parameters [@Saltelli2010]; a variance-based extension (Sobol indices) is straightforward in principle and is left for future work. The present analysis is therefore a lower-bound robustness check rather than a full sensitivity decomposition. Six model parameters were each varied ±30% from their base values: training threshold (0.30), skill gain per attempt (0.06), skill gain per training step (0.08), cull fraction (0.25), cap growth rate (0.005), and mutation standard deviation (0.04). Each of the 12 perturbed conditions was run under 3 seeds per scenario, yielding 18 parameter conditions per outcome metric.

**Both confirmatory effects are robust across the six-parameter sweep.** The peaked-profile per-domain Gini exceeded the broad-profile Gini in all 18 of 18 parameter conditions (H2, 100% directional consistency), and the peaked-profile failure rate fell below the broad-profile failure rate in all 18 conditions (the reversed H1, 100% directional consistency). Neither confirmatory effect depends on the specific calibration of any of the six swept parameters: across the ±30% sweep of training threshold, skill-gain-per-attempt, skill-gain-per-training-step, cull fraction, cap-growth rate, and mutation standard deviation, the direction never flips. Both the reversed H1 and the H2 concentration effect are structural consequences of the skill-distribution shape, not products of a particular heuristic-parameter setting.

### Type B parameters: α and β {#sec-sensitivity-type-b}

The Type B comparison (@sec-type-b-results) fixed the Rescorla–Wagner parameters at $\alpha = 0.10$ (learning rate) and $\beta = 3.0$ (softmax inverse temperature). To test whether the Type B finding is sensitive to those choices, both parameters were swept at five levels each (α ∈ {0.05, 0.075, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20}; β ∈ {1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 4.5, 6.0}) with the other held at base, yielding 240 simulations under 8 seeds per cell at 300 steps. **The reversed H1** (Peaked < Broad failure rate) holds at *every* one of the 10 swept levels — $d(\text{P},\text{B})$ is negative throughout, range −0.21 to −2.29. **H2** (Peaked > Broad per-domain Gini) holds at 9 of the 10 levels — $d(\text{P},\text{B})$ positive across the entire α sweep and at β ≤ 4.5 (range 0.21–1.51) — with the single exception β = 6.0, where it collapses to $d = -0.38$ (n.s.). Statistical significance varied with the modest N = 8 per cell, but the directional finding is robust across the practically relevant range of α and β. The reversed-H1 claim and the H2 claim are therefore not artefacts of the specific Rescorla–Wagner calibration, with the one caveat noted below.

**Exploratory finding (Type B): H2 collapses at high softmax temperature β.** The β sweep is informative beyond a directional-robustness check. H2 is positive and meaningful across the low-to-mid β range but collapses at the high end: at β = 6.0 the effect goes to $d = -0.38$ (n.s.), the only direction-flip in the entire 10-level sweep. The mechanism is interpretable. At high β the softmax is near-greedy on $\operatorname{argmax}(U)$, so agents in *both* scenarios concentrate on whichever single domain has accumulated the most reward — the structural difference between Peaked and Broad washes out because both populations end up tightly concentrated on a single learned-best domain rather than expressing their underlying skill distribution's broader shape. The precise shape of the H2–β curve at the lower end is noisy at N = 8 and should not be over-read; the robust, interpretable feature is the high-β collapse. This identifies the operational regime in which the feedback-emergent component of H2 (@sec-type-b-results) actually emerges: feedback-driven concentration requires a softmax peaked enough to express domain-utility differences but *not so peaked* that it degenerates to greedy argmax selection. The finding is exploratory — observed post hoc in the sensitivity data, with the mechanism interpretable from the softmax form — and identifies a parameter regime worth a denser, higher-seed sweep in future work.

# Discussion

## What the Model Demonstrates

<!-- VOICE OWNERSHIP: H1/H2/H3/H4 paragraphs were heavily rewritten across tiers (most recently 103291b). The section is longer than it needs to be and structured around AI-style "honest reading" / "calibrated structural claim" framings. Significant rewrite recommended. -->


The results provide a direct answer to each of the four research questions — and the answer to the first one is the opposite of what was hypothesised.

**H1 — refuted, and reversed.** H1 predicted that the Peaked scenario would fail *more* than Broad. Under the confound-corrected (mean-skill, gap) parameterisation the data show the reverse: Peaked fails *less* (.561 vs. .652; *d* = −2.65). The reversal traces to a confound in an earlier parameterisation (@sec-scenarios): when peak and non-peak means were specified directly, a more peaked profile also carried lower total competence, mixing a shape effect with a magnitude effect. Holding total competence constant and varying only dispersion isolates the shape effect, which runs the other way — concentrating a fixed competence budget reduces replication failure. The effect has two components. *Immediate*: concentrating competence raises the proficiency at which a researcher works in their niche (0.68 vs. 0.482), and Equation 1's similarity term rewards niche proficiency, so peaked-profile researchers succeed more on the attempts they make from step one. *Cumulative*: a Peaked community contains high-skill summits whose published work carries high complexity, so the whole community assimilates toward that advanced work and its mean skill climbs over the run (to 0.41, vs. 0.35 for Broad and 0.33 for Flat — @sec-mechanism). Concentrated competence is, in this sense, a public good — a few deep specialists raise the frontier everyone else learns from. The original H1 was an artefact of the mean-skill confound; the corrected finding is that concentration of competence reduces replication failure, both immediately and cumulatively. This is a stronger and more surprising claim, and it is unusually robust — present at the base architecture (ablation Layer 1), at every ablation layer, under the Type B action-selection architecture, and at every level of both sensitivity sweeps (@sec-ablation, @sec-type-b-results, @sec-sensitivity). That a pre-registered hypothesis was refuted by correcting a confound the analysis itself surfaced is a feature of the work's method, not a weakness of its result: the model was used to audit its own parameterisation, and the audit changed the answer.

**H2 — supported.** Greater publication concentration in the Peaked scenario was confirmed (*d* = 1.41), and it is the cleanest of the confirmatory findings. The Type B comparison (@sec-type-b-results) decomposes it: replacing the skill-bias action-selection rule (Equation 6) with softmax over Rescorla–Wagner-learned utility drops the effect from *d* = 1.41 to *d* = 0.90, so the skill-bias rule contributes roughly *d* ≈ 0.5 and the success → reward → utility feedback loop contributes the larger *d* ≈ 0.9. H2 is therefore partly architectural and substantially feedback-emergent, with the feedback component dominant. The Flat control sharpens it in the orthogonal direction: with no skill heterogeneity the Gini falls to .082, well below both Peaked and Broad, so concentration requires skill heterogeneity as a necessary condition and scales monotonically with dispersion. Domain concentration is the model's most robust *confirmatory* result — supported in direction as pre-registered, robust across architecture and parameter sweeps, and decomposable into interpretable components.

**H3 — concentrated competence raises both the ceiling and the inequality of careers.** Peaked-profile researchers accumulate substantially more reputation than broad-profile researchers (11.61 vs. 9.00; *d* = 2.61). The mechanism is transparent: reputation is paced by the highest-quality work a researcher can produce, which is bounded by peak skill, and the mean-constant design makes peak skill vary between scenarios (0.68 vs. 0.482). H3 therefore serves two purposes simultaneously: it confirms that the reparameterisation behaves as intended (concentrating a fixed competence budget raises the ceiling on individual achievement), and it documents a substantive finding — that the same structural variable shaping community-level outcomes (H1, H2) also shapes the *distribution* of career outcomes. The reputation *variance* in the Peaked scenario is substantially higher (56.9 vs. 39.5), so concentration of competence produces not only a higher mean reputation but a more unequal one: a few researchers benefit greatly from their peak proficiency while others, with the same total competence budget, do not.

**H4 — null.** Debunk impact rate did not differ between scenarios (*d* = 0.20, n.s.). Under the gradient-aware debunk threshold (Equation 5a) and the quadratic-in-gradient instability boost (Equation 5), debunking is a rare, low-impact event: both mechanisms restrict successful debunks to genuinely unstable, steep-landscape work, and most published models settle at stable plateau positions. Community structure does not measurably affect how much reputation is lost to debunking. The structural-sheltering intuition behind H4 is not contradicted — it is simply that, with debunking rare overall, the scenarios do not separate on this metric.

**Stepping back: how the four results speak to the Introduction's claim.** The work supplies an empirical answer to the Introduction's framing of *skill distribution* as the third, underexamined infrastructure layer of scientific-community functioning, alongside the statistical-and-procedural and theoretical-formalism layers. The two robust findings — the reversed H1 and the confirmed H2 — both show that the *shape* of the skill distribution, holding total competence constant, is sufficient to move system-level outcomes: how broadly a fixed competence budget is spread determines both the community's replication failure rate and the concentration of its publication landscape. H3 confirms that the same structural variable also sets the ceiling on individual careers. Taken together the results establish skill distribution as a tractable structural variable for formal modelling — one that complements rather than competes with the statistical-norm and theoretical-formalism lenses, and that the existing reform literature has so far left implicit. The direction of the H1 effect was not what the project predicted; that the corrected answer is sharper than the original hypothesis is the clearest demonstration that the variable is worth modelling formally rather than reasoning about verbally.

## Relation to Existing Models

The present model is situated within a growing tradition of agent-based models of scientific communities and can be evaluated against three prior contributions it draws on directly. Mapped onto the three-layer infrastructure framing of the Introduction, each prior work addresses a different layer: @McElreath2015 the statistical-and-procedural layer (how statistical parameters propagate to community-level reliability), @WeisbergMuldoon2009 the cognitive-labor layer (how heterogeneous research strategies span theoretical space), and @Devezer2019 the methodological-diversity layer (how the mix of research orientations affects truth convergence). The present work adds the *skill-distribution* layer — who is competent to evaluate what, and how broadly that competence is spread — as a distinct structural variable, and shows that this layer interacts non-trivially with the dynamics those prior works study.

@McElreath2015 demonstrate mathematically that under realistic parameters for base rate, power, and false-positive rate, a field's aggregate reliability is determined by the dynamics of publication and replication rather than by individual researcher intentions. The present model extends this insight by giving individual researchers heterogeneous skill profiles and allowing those profiles to shape which models get attempted and with what probability of success. The result is consistent with their population-level analysis but shows that the distribution of skill — not only the statistical parameters of tests — is an independent determinant of aggregate replication rates.

@Devezer2019 show that epistemic diversity is more important than any single research strategy: populations with a mix of conservative exploiters and bold explorers discover truth faster and are more robust than populations dominated by either type alone. The present model does not directly vary exploration strategy but varies skill *dispersion* at constant total competence. Here the relationship to @Devezer2019 is more nuanced than a simple "diversity helps" reading would suggest. The present results show that *concentration* of competence reduces replication failure and the *broad* (more even) distribution produces less concentrated publication landscapes — so on the failure-rate metric, concentration is favoured, while on the concentration metric, breadth is favoured. The two findings together caution against treating "diversity" as monolithically good: which distribution is preferable depends on which system-level outcome is in view. What both this work and @Devezer2019 share is the deeper point that population-structure variables, not only individual behaviour, determine community-level epistemic outcomes.

@WeisbergMuldoon2009 model the division of cognitive labour on an epistemic landscape and show that different research strategies are complementary: the community as a whole explores a larger region than any individual strategy would by itself. The action-selection mechanism in the present model (Equations 3 and 6) captures a similar logic: researchers are not uniform in their orientation but are probabilistically pulled toward regions of the domain space where their skills give them comparative advantage. The skill-bias term operationalises precisely the kind of local landscape navigation that @WeisbergMuldoon2009 describe, and the confirmation of H1 and H2 suggests that when skill distributions are too narrow, this local navigation produces the epistemic monoculture they warned against.

## Limitations: What the Model Cannot Tell Us {#sec-limitations}

<!-- VOICE OWNERSHIP: Extended in tier 4 (commit aa3e1f7) with new "third limitation" paragraph on the epistemic landscape. That paragraph in particular is AI-drafted. The first two limitations are older and may already be in your voice — verify. -->


Any computational model carries a gap between what it formalises and what it claims to represent, and the present model is no exception.

The most important limitation concerns what the confirmatory results do and do not establish. The directional results follow transparently from how skill enters the model's equations: the reversed H1 from the success-probability rule (Equation 1) rewarding niche proficiency, H2 partly from the skill-bias action-selection rule (Equation 6). This is inherent to any formal model — a model's outputs are consequences of its equations — and the present work quantifies it rather than denies it. The layer ablation (@sec-ablation) shows both effects are present at the base architecture; the Type B comparison (@sec-type-b-results) shows the reversed H1 survives the removal of Equation 6 entirely and decomposes H2 into architectural and feedback-emergent components. The directional results are therefore traceable to specific equations, and the work makes that traceability explicit. The genuine limitation is one of scope, not hidden circularity: the experiment does not test whether skill concentration affects *real* communities; it quantifies the magnitude and dynamics of these effects under a particular formalisation. A reader looking for evidence that real-world specialisation reduces real-world replication failure should not take the reversed H1 as such evidence. What the model contributes is a controlled estimate of effect size given the assumed mechanism, a decomposition of architectural components, and a demonstration — through the corrected confound (@sec-scenarios) — that formal modelling can audit its own parameterisation in ways verbal theorising cannot.

The most fundamental limitation concerns the mapping from model parameters to real scientific communities. The choice of 50 researchers, 10 domains, and a per-researcher mean skill of 0.32 is not derived from empirical measurements of actual psychological departments; these values were chosen to produce a functioning simulation with discriminable scenarios. This is not unusual in this class of model — @Smaldino2017 notes that the purpose of a model is to demonstrate that a mechanism is *sufficient* to produce a phenomenon, not to quantitatively reproduce measured rates. Nevertheless, the proximity of the simulated Peaked-scenario failure rate (≈ 56%) to the 61% non-replication rate reported by @OpenScienceCollaboration2015 is suggestive rather than confirmatory; the model is not calibrated to that figure, and the comparison should not be read as empirical validation.

A second limitation, discussed in the Introduction, concerns the theory crisis [@Eronen2021] and deserves a more substantial engagement than a citation. @Eronen2021 identify three structural features of psychological phenomena that frustrate cumulative theorising even before any incentive or replication issue arises: interventions are *fat-handed* (a manipulation intended to affect one variable simultaneously affects several), construct validity is chronically weak (the same label denotes operationally distinct things across labs), and the field lacks robust theory-independent regularities of the kind that anchor formal theorising in physics. The present model's `actual_truthfulness` construct presupposes that none of these obtain — that there is a determinate fact of the matter about whether a finding replicates, that the same measurement strategy applied by different competent researchers would converge, and that the phenomenon under study is stable enough for replication to be a coherent test rather than an ambiguous one. In psychology, this presupposition is, by Eronen and Bringmann's argument, frequently false. The model therefore addresses the *publication-bias* problem (where the underlying phenomenon is real but the reported effect is inflated) more squarely than it addresses the *theory-crisis* problem (where the phenomenon may not have a stable identity to be replicated against). To engage the latter would require fundamentally different model machinery: actual_truthfulness would need to be context-dependent (varying with measurement strategy or population), and the success-probability rule would need to incorporate the possibility that two replication attempts could both succeed and both produce different effects, neither of which would be the "right" answer. Such a model would speak more directly to the theory crisis but would also lose the clean falsification logic that makes the present model's H1/H2 contrasts interpretable. The choice made here — to assume away the theory-crisis question in order to study the publication-bias question — is a deliberate scope decision, not an oversight, but it bounds what the model can claim about psychology specifically. The findings translate most cleanly to fields where the phenomena are stable enough that "did this replicate?" has a determinate answer.

A third limitation concerns the epistemic landscape itself. The Gaussian-mixture surface introduced in @sec-landscape is presented in the Methods as a piece of model architecture, but it is also — and this should be acknowledged plainly — a substantive theoretical claim about how scientific theory-space is structured. The model assumes that domains have stable attractors (plateaus representing well-established paradigms), that high-gradient theoretical positions are systematically less reliable (peak edges representing cutting-edge but unstable theory), and that mature research programmes converge on stable plateau anchors via the step-toward-stable dynamic. None of these assumptions is empirically validated in this work; they are inherited from the @WeisbergMuldoon2009 epistemic-landscape framework as a working theoretical commitment. Five downstream model behaviours depend on this commitment (replication probability, debunking vulnerability, salience decay, publication-bias inflation, and action-selection attractiveness — see @sec-landscape), so the landscape is doing substantial structural work, not merely decorating the simulation. A reader who rejects the landscape framework should expect different model behaviour; a reader who accepts it should recognise that some of the paper's results (the debunk dynamics, the spatial pattern of active models in Figure \ref{fig:landscape}) depend on it. The ablation analysis (@sec-ablation) quantifies the magnitude of this dependence rather than leaving it implicit: removing the landscape leaves both the reversed H1 and the H2 effect essentially intact, so the landscape shapes intermediate dynamics but does not drive the headline findings.

A fourth limitation is the binary character of the Peaked–Broad contrast. Real scientific communities are not composed uniformly of one type; they contain both, in varying proportions, alongside other forms of heterogeneity (interdisciplinary training, methodological diversity, seniority gradients) that the present model does not capture. The two-scenario design is appropriate for an initial investigation of the direction and magnitude of the effect but cannot characterise the full distribution of outcomes across mixed communities.

Finally, the evolutionary selection mechanism is a substantial simplification of academic career dynamics. Researchers are removed and replaced based purely on recent reputation gain, and new researchers are drawn as mutated copies of elite researchers. This captures the broad competitive pressure of academic hiring but omits many real features: the role of institutional prestige, funding constraints, mentorship, collaborative networks, and geographic concentration. These omissions are deliberate — adding them would increase complexity without changing the key manipulation — but they limit the model's ability to speak to concrete policy recommendations about hiring or training practices.

A sixth limitation, related to but distinct from the architectural-traceability point made above, is that the Type B variant (@sec-architecture) addresses only one of three possible architectural commitments. The taxonomy in @sec-architecture distinguishes Type A (structural specialisation, encoded directly in the action-selection rule), Type B (emergent specialisation through Rescorla–Wagner learning, where concentration arises from a success → reward → utility feedback loop), and Type C (institutional reinforcement, where concentration emerges from prestige cascades, citation visibility, and lab-level selection of productive niches). Type C is implemented here only in partial form — the lab fingerprint drift mechanism and the social-learning bonus capture aspects of it, but a fully institutional model would replace researcher-level utility with lab-level prestige and citation flow. Such a model would speak more directly to sociological accounts of science [@Crane1972; @Whitley2000] but lies beyond the scope of this thesis.

A seventh limitation concerns model complexity itself. The simulation has more moving parts than canonical parsimony-prized ABMs of scientific communities (e.g., @Smaldino2016 operates with on the order of five free parameters; the present model has roughly thirty), and a fair examiner could ask whether some of that complexity is doing structural work or merely accumulating fidelity. The honest answer has two parts. First, most additional mechanisms are interpretable — each is anchored to a specific literature claim (Matthew effect to @Merton1968, social learning to @Crane1972, career stages to @Petersen2011, misconduct rates to @Fang2012, the epistemic landscape to @WeisbergMuldoon2009, skill assimilation to @Anderson1982) rather than being a fit constant. Second, the model actively tests which mechanisms matter through the layer ablation (@sec-ablation), the Flat control (@sec-control), and the Type B comparison (@sec-type-b-results), and reports separately which findings are necessary, which are calibrated, and which are partly architectural. Some mechanisms — the breakthrough salience shock at $\times 0.35$, fingerprint drift's asymmetric 0.2%/0.1% constants, the dual misconduct-and-pressure pathways — are defensible but not load-bearing for the headline findings and could in principle be removed or simplified without affecting H1 or H2 in direction. The model is best read as a *core* of necessary mechanisms surrounded by a calibrated breadth chosen for fidelity to the literature; it is not a single integrated mechanism whose every parameter is doing structural work.

## Implications and Their Limits

<!-- VOICE OWNERSHIP: Rewritten in tier 4 cluster C (commit aa3e1f7) to remove policy creep. Heavy hedging language ("the work is consistent with the view that..."). The hedging is the right move; the wording is AI-style — rephrase in your idiom. -->


What does this work imply for the reform agenda in psychology? The honest answer is: less than the simulation results, taken at face value, might suggest. The model's H1 and H2 findings concern a stylised population of fifty researchers, ten domains, and a particular formalisation of skill, replication, and publication dynamics over 300 simulated steps. Translating those findings into recommendations about real institutions, real career structures, or real training requires assumptions about the mapping between model and world that the simulation itself does not validate. Three points can nonetheless be raised cautiously.

First, the work suggests that *skill distribution* is worth taking seriously as a structural variable in formal models of scientific communities, alongside the incentive and statistical variables that dominate the existing meta-scientific literature. Most reform proposals operate on the statistical interface between a researcher and a result — pre-registration, registered reports, open data. The present model is consistent with the view that the *skill interface* — whether a researcher has the competency to meaningfully evaluate work outside their primary domain — is a tractable additional axis for formal analysis. That is a claim about *what to model*, not a claim about *what to do* in a real psychology department.

Second, the H2 finding (and the Flat-control sharpening) shows that domain concentration emerges from skill heterogeneity within the model's dynamics. Domain concentration is not itself a pathology; depth of specialisation produces high-truthfulness work in the model and presumably also in real domains. What the model adds to the discussion is a quantitative account of how concentration scales with the shape of the skill distribution — useful as a starting point for empirical investigation rather than as a prescription. Whether real scientific communities operate in the regime where these dynamics dominate is a question the model cannot answer.

Third, any practical reading should be hedged rather than prescriptive. The model is consistent with the view that maintaining cross-domain coverage — whether through methodologists, meta-scientists, or replication infrastructure — is structurally valuable. It does not show that this is the right reform priority, that it would work in practice, or that the magnitudes observed in simulation translate to real institutional settings. The Gini undershoot relative to empirical publication distributions (@sec-validation) is one explicit reminder that the model's quantitative regime does not match the empirical one in all respects. Readers who want to draw policy conclusions from this work should treat it as a tractable formal lens for thinking about skill heterogeneity in scientific communities, not as evidence about which reforms will succeed.

One analytic observation connects the model's bias mechanism to a wider literature: the gap between *reported* and *actual* truthfulness has the formal structure of an information-asymmetry problem [@Spence1973; @Akerlof1970], with low-reputation senders inflating most and the largest reported-vs-actual gap concentrated at peak landscape positions — the model's analogue of adverse selection where buyers find quality hardest to verify. The implementation falls short of a full strategic signalling equilibrium (no costly signal, no buyer withdrawal); what it captures is the *pre-equilibrium pressure* under which systematically inflated signals can persist absent any individual bad faith. Making inflation explicitly quality-dependent, in the manner of classical signalling models, is the natural extension and is taken up in the next section.

**Closing the loop.** The Introduction identified three infrastructure layers — *statistical-and-procedural*, *theoretical-formalism*, and *skill-distribution* — and named the third as the layer this thesis isolates. The empirical results land squarely on it: skill-distribution shape is sufficient to produce both the headline replication and the concentration patterns, and the patterns survive a meaningful change in the action-selection rule (Type B) and plausible variation in its parameters. The contribution is not a policy claim or a calibration to any specific psychology department; it is a demonstration that a previously underexamined structural variable — how broadly competence is spread across the people doing the work — admits formal modelling and shapes the system-level outcomes the meta-scientific literature already cares about. The communicative infrastructure of a discipline includes the human capacity to evaluate work outside one's primary expertise, and that capacity is itself a function of how skill is distributed. Treating that distribution as a tractable model variable opens a class of questions the existing meta-scientific tools cannot address.

## Recommendations for Future Research

Several extensions to the present model would substantially sharpen its conclusions. The most important is varying the *proportion* of peaked- and broad-profile researchers within a single community, rather than comparing homogeneous scenarios. A mixed community might show non-linear effects: because the present results indicate that concentrated competence lowers replication failure while broad competence spreads publication activity more evenly, a mixed community could plausibly capture both benefits — a core of specialists sustaining a low community failure rate, with a minority of broad-profile researchers maintaining cross-domain coverage. Whether such a mix is achievable, or whether the two outcomes trade off against each other, is exactly the question a proportion-sweep would answer, and it would yield a more actionable picture than the present homogeneous-scenario comparison.

A second extension concerns the publication bias mechanism. The present model treats bias inflation as a fixed draw from a distribution at the time of publication, driven by researcher-level competitive pressure. A theoretically motivated refinement would make inflation additionally dependent on a model's actual quality: in signaling equilibria [@Spence1973; @Akerlof1970], low-quality senders have the strongest incentive to inflate because the gap between their true quality and desired perception is largest. Implementing quality-dependent inflation — where the bias mean decreases with actual truthfulness — would more closely reproduce the adverse-selection structure described above and allow the model to test whether the worst work is systematically over-reported relative to work of genuine quality. In reality, the magnitude of publication bias is also a function of field-level norms: when journals publish only surprising results, the expected inflation is larger than when null results are valued. Coupling the bias distribution to a parameter representing publication standards would allow the model to examine how norm reform interacts with both skill distribution and signal quality.

Third, the model currently treats domain boundaries as fixed and impermeable: a researcher's domain skills are real-valued but the domains themselves do not merge or split. Real scientific disciplines do both: cognitive neuroscience absorbed parts of experimental psychology and biology; social media research created a new domain from parts of communication studies, computer science, and sociology. Introducing domain evolution — mergers that require cross-domain proficiency, splits that reward concentration — would make the model more realistic and might sharpen the specialist-generalist contrast.

Finally, the present model treats researchers as acting independently, but scientific work is predominantly collaborative. Extending the model to include co-authorship and inter-lab partnerships would open a third level of analysis between the individual and the aggregate community. Crucially, skill distribution shapes not only research output but the *possibility* of collaboration in the first place: the similarity term in Equation 1 — the Pearson correlation between two skill profiles — provides a natural operationalisation of mutual intelligibility, since researchers whose profiles are largely non-overlapping can engage with each other's work only superficially. A specialist community would on this account be a landscape of parallel siloes with near-zero cross-domain intelligibility, while a generalist community would sustain a denser network of viable partnerships — precisely the lateral knowledge transfer that the Introduction identifies as the communicative infrastructure of cumulative science. Modelling this explicitly would allow the question of whether targeted bridging — a small number of deliberately cross-trained generalists embedded in a specialist community — can prevent the epistemic fragmentation that the present results suggest is a structural consequence of narrow skill distributions.

A related methodological completion is to perform leave-one-out parameter recovery for the Rescorla–Wagner parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$, paralleling the recovery analysis already done for the manipulated gap (@sec-validation). The sensitivity sweep on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ already shows the Type B results are not narrowly tuned to those values (@sec-sensitivity-type-b); a recovery analysis would additionally establish that the outcome metrics carry enough information to identify $\alpha$ and $\beta$ separately, completing the methodological story for the Type B variant. The marginal value is small — these are nuisance parameters of the Type B architecture rather than the experimental IV — but the analysis is straightforward and is left as future work.

A further refinement concerns the *skill-growth* mechanism. In the present model skill grows only through assimilation toward existing model complexity (Equation 7): researchers learn by engaging with work that is more advanced than their current level, and the community's skill frontier advances only as fast as its most advanced published work. This is a frontier-limited learning model, and it has a clear consequence — visible in the skill-frontier divergence of @sec-mechanism — that a community with no high-skill summit (the Flat scenario) barely advances. A natural alternative is *experience-based learning*: a small skill increment from the act of doing research itself, independent of whether the work engaged with is more advanced than the researcher. Adding such a term would allow even a flat community to advance through accumulated practice, and would let the model distinguish "learning by studying advanced work" from "learning by doing" — two channels that the current single-mechanism formulation conflates. Whether experience-based learning materially changes the H1 ordering, or merely raises all three scenarios' trajectories in parallel, is an empirical question for a future version.

A more local refinement concerns the *functional form* of the debunkability mechanism (Equation 5). The present model implements a quadratic-in-gradient instability boost, $\propto \tan^2\theta$, derived from a first-order perturbation-variance argument (see Methods). A natural further step is the **curvature-augmented** form: adding a Laplacian term $|\nabla^2 t|$ to capture the *spikiness* of the landscape independent of slope. Sharp local peaks have high curvature; long uniform slopes have low curvature. The quadratic-in-gradient form already distinguishes these to first order, but a curvature term would do so more directly — at the cost of an additional numerical-second-derivative evaluation per call and one more parameter (the curvature weight). Whether the extra structural commitment earns its place is an empirical question for a more mature version of the model; the quadratic form was chosen here as the formulation with the cleanest derivation and no added free parameter.
